section.title: Against Egypt
section.sectionRationale: Egypt, Judah's tempting but unreliable ally against Babylon, is judged here for the same root sin as Tyre: proud self sufficiency, pictured as Pharaoh's boast that the Nile, and Egypt's whole existence, belongs to himself alone. The chapter promises Egypt's desolation, a limited exile and partial restoration, and closes by paying Babylon with Egypt's spoils as wages for her long labor against Tyre.
section.thesis: Egypt's pride in self sufficient power, and Judah's foolish trust in that broken reed of an ally, both fall before the LORD who alone raises up and humbles nations, though even in judgment He measures Egypt's exile and leaves room for a modest, humbled future.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Pharaoh's boast that the Nile is his own answered by God's judgment and Egypt's failure as Israel's ally; the promise of forty years of desolation and scattering followed by a limited restoration to a lowly kingdom; and Egypt's wealth given to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for his long, unpaid labor against Tyre.

units.label: Pharaoh's boast answered
units.note: the Nile is mine, I made it

verses.text: In the tenth year, on the twelfth day of the tenth month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, set your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt and prophesy against him and against all Egypt.

Speak to him and tell him that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Pharaoh king of Egypt, O great {{tannin|monster}} who lies among his rivers, who says, 'The Nile is mine; I made it myself.'
But I will put hooks in your jaws and cause the fish of your streams to cling to your scales. I will haul you up out of your rivers, and all the fish of your streams will cling to your scales.

I will leave you in the desert, you and all the fish of your streams. You will fall on the open field and will not be taken away or gathered for burial. I have given you as food to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the air.
Then all the people of Egypt will know that I am the LORD. For you were only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel.
When Israel took hold of you with their hands, you splintered, tearing all their shoulders; when they leaned on you, you broke, and their backs were wrenched.
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will bring a sword against you and cut off from you man and beast.
The land of Egypt will become a desolate wasteland. Then they will know that I am the LORD. Because you said, 'The Nile is mine; I made it,'
therefore I am against you and against your rivers. I will turn the land of Egypt into a ruin, a desolate wasteland from Migdol to Syene, and as far as the border of Cush.
No foot of man or beast will pass through, and it will be uninhabited for forty years.

units.label: Forty years, then a lowly kingdom

verses.text: I will make the land of Egypt a desolation among desolate lands, and her cities will lie desolate for forty years among the ruined cities. And I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the countries.
For this is what the Lord GOD says: At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered.
I will restore Egypt from captivity and bring them back to the land of Pathros, the land of their origin. There they will be a lowly kingdom.
Egypt will be the lowliest of kingdoms and will never again exalt itself above the nations. For I will diminish Egypt so that it will never again rule over the nations.
Egypt will never again be an object of trust for the house of Israel, but will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.”
In the twenty-seventh year, on the first day of the first month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

“Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon caused his army to labor strenuously against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder made raw. But he and his army received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it.

Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will carry off its wealth, seize its spoil, and remove its plunder. This will be the wages for his army.
I have given him the land of Egypt as the reward for his labor, because it was done for Me, declares the Lord GOD.
In that day I will cause a {{qeren|horn}} to sprout for the house of Israel, and I will open your mouth to speak among them. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

tannin.gloss: A great sea or river monster, sometimes a crocodile, elsewhere used of the primeval chaos monster subdued by God at creation. Pharaoh, who claims to have made the Nile himself, is cast as this very monster, a creature God alone made and can just as easily haul out and destroy.

qeren.gloss: A horn, a common biblical image for strength, dignity, or a raised, victorious power, often associated with kings or deliverers. The promise that a horn will sprout for Israel points to a future restoration of strength precisely when Egypt, her former source of misplaced trust, is most thoroughly humbled.

basic.context: This chapter opens the Egypt sequence, chapters 29 to 32, with Pharaoh judged for the same root sin already condemned in Tyre, proud self sufficiency, here expressed in his boast that he made the Nile himself. The chapter also names Egypt's specific failure as an ally, a staff of reeds that splintered and wounded Israel's hand rather than supporting it, and closes with a striking historical note: Egypt's wealth given to Nebuchadnezzar as overdue wages for his long, costly siege of Tyre.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes real, dated historical judgments: Egypt's devastation under Babylonian pressure, a genuine period of decline and diminished influence following this era, and a specific historical transaction in which Egypt's resources compensated Babylon for the Tyre campaign. The forty years of desolation and Egypt's promised lowly restoration describe an actual historical trajectory of decline for Egypt's regional power, not merely a symbolic idea, even where the precise chronology of 'forty years' is debated among historians.
basic.originalLanguages: Pharaoh, who claims 'I made the Nile myself,' is called a tannin, a great river monster, the very kind of primeval chaos creature Scripture elsewhere says only God can subdue, an ironic reversal of his boast. And the chapter closes with a promise that a qeren, a horn, a picture of restored strength and dignity, will sprout for Israel exactly when her former, misplaced source of trust lies humbled.
basic.typology: Egypt cast down as a defeated sea monster, later restored only as 'the lowliest of kingdoms,' anticipates the wider biblical pattern of every proud human power being subdued, while the horn promised to Israel points forward to the ultimate horn of salvation raised up in the house of David, Luke 1:69, Christ Himself.
basic.christ: Egypt's proud self sufficiency, 'the Nile is mine, I made it,' is answered by the God who alone made the Nile and everything in it; where human empires boast of self made power, Christ alone is the true horn of salvation, raised not from human strength but from God's own faithfulness to His covenant people, Luke 1:68-69.
basic.god: God is sovereign over the nations' rise and fall, using even one pagan empire, Babylon, to discipline another, Egypt, and paying Babylon's very real, uncompensated military labor with Egypt's own wealth, showing His justice attends to detail even in international affairs between nations who do not know Him.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 19 and Jeremiah 46 give companion oracles against Egypt. 2 Kings 18:21 and Isaiah 36:6 both use the image of Egypt as a splintering reed of a staff, a broken support for anyone who leans on her, closely matching this chapter's verse 6 to 7. Luke 1:68-69 speaks of God raising up 'a horn of salvation' in the house of David, echoing this chapter's closing promise for Israel.
basic.oneStory: Egypt's proud self sufficiency and Israel's foolish trust in her as an ally both fall before the LORD, who alone sustains and topples nations; yet even here, in the very chapter that humbles Egypt to her lowest point, God promises a horn of restored strength for Israel, a promise finally and fully answered in the true horn of salvation, Jesus Christ, raised up in the house of David.

context.literary:
The chapter is built from six dated or datable units, and the dates matter. Verse 1 places the first word in the tenth year, tenth month, twelfth day of Jehoiachin's exile, while Jerusalem was under siege, which fixes the oracle to the very season of the siege. Verses 3 to 9a are one judgment speech, verses 9b to 16 a second, and verses 17 to 21 a postscript dated to the twenty-seventh year, the latest date anywhere in Ezekiel. The collection of Egyptian oracles in chapters 29 to 32 is therefore arranged by theme, not by calendar: the last word of this chapter was spoken sixteen years after the next oracle begins.

The first speech works by a reversal of hunting. The river creature who boasts of owning the Nile is the one hooked in the jaw, dragged out of the water and left unburied on the open field, verses 3 to 5. Her fish stick to her scales, so her whole people go with her. The second half of the speech turns from the monster to the reed, verses 6 to 7, a switch from Egypt's own pride to Egypt's effect on others, and it hinges on the formula 'Then all the people of Egypt will know that I am the LORD,' verse 6. That recognition formula returns at verses 9, 16 and 21, and it frames each unit as a lesson to be learned.

Verses 10 to 12 sketch the whole land from end to end, Migdol to Syene, and verses 13 to 16 answer with a limited rescue. The structure ruin, scattering, regathering, humbling is deliberately lopsided: the restoration is real but is described entirely in terms of how small it will be.
context.historical:
In the tenth year of exile, the winter of 588 to 587 BC by the usual reckoning, Zedekiah had rebelled against Babylon and was relying on Egypt. Ezekiel 17:15 records his envoys asking Egypt for horses and a large army. Jeremiah 37:5 to 8 describes the result: Pharaoh's army marched out, the Chaldeans lifted the siege for a time, and Jeremiah warned that Egypt would simply go home and the city would burn. The 'staff of reeds' of verse 6 is therefore not a figure for a distant disappointment but a description of what had happened within living memory, and what was happening that very season.

The Pharaoh of the day, Hophra in Jeremiah 44:30, is called king of Egypt without a personal name here, because the oracle addresses the institution. Egyptian royal ideology presented the king as the guarantor of the Nile's flood, on which all agriculture depended, so the boast 'The Nile is mine; I made it myself' states the claim of the throne in the first person. Migdol lay at the north-eastern frontier and Syene, modern Aswan, at the southern, so verse 10 names the whole length of the country, and Pathros in verse 14 is the southern region, Upper Egypt, known to Jeremiah 44:1 as a place where Jewish refugees settled.

The postscript of verses 17 to 21 comes from about 571 BC. By then Jerusalem had fallen and Nebuchadnezzar had spent years pressing Tyre, which Ezekiel had said he would take, Ezekiel 26:7. The siege had worn out his men without paying them. Ezekiel does not hide this disappointment. He interprets it as God's own payroll: Egypt is the wage.
context.canonical:
Egypt is the Bible's oldest oppressor, and this chapter is one of many places where she is put back in her place. The first Pharaoh to oppose God asked, 'Who is the LORD?' in Exodus 5:2, and the plagues struck at the Nile directly, turning its waters to blood, Exodus 7:19. Ezekiel's image of the monster hooked and hauled out of the river replays that contest. Where the Exodus story had God draw Israel out of Egypt, here He draws Egypt's king out of his own river.

The reed image is shared with Isaiah and the Kings narrative. The Assyrian envoy mocked Hezekiah for trusting 'that splintered reed of a staff,' 2 Kings 18:21, and Isaiah warned that 'Pharaoh's protection will become your shame,' Isaiah 30:3. Ezekiel's twist is to claim the mockery for God and give it a moral edge: leaning on Egypt was a sin that Israel must remember, verse 16.

The promise of a limited restoration for Egypt has a surprising echo. Jeremiah 46:26 says that after Babylon's conquest, 'Egypt will be inhabited as in days of old,' and Isaiah 19:22 to 25 goes much further, with Egypt struck and healed and called 'My people.' The closing 'horn' of verse 21 is taken up in Hannah's song, 1 Samuel 2:10, in Psalm 132:17, and by Zechariah in Luke 1:69, so a promise tucked into an oracle against Egypt becomes a bridge to the birth of Jesus.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's first hearers were exiles who had watched Judah's leaders run to Egypt, and some of them were quietly hoping Egypt would yet turn the war. The oracle tells them that the hope is misplaced and, worse, that it is sin. The recurring 'they will know that I am the LORD' means that the purpose of Egypt's fall is revelation, not only punishment. Even Egypt will be taught who made the river.

The chapter also protects the exiles from two opposite errors. One is despair, the thought that the empires are too big for God. The other is revenge, the thought that Egypt's ruin is simply deserved and finished. The oracle answers both: God hooks the monster, and God also settles Egypt again in Pathros, small but alive, verses 13 to 15. The postscript gives the discouraged prophet and his people a concrete assurance that nothing done 'for Me,' verse 20, goes unrewarded, even work by a pagan king that did not seem to achieve its goal. And it ends on a seed of hope for Israel and a restored voice for Ezekiel, whose mouth God had promised to open, Ezekiel 3:26 to 27 and 24:27.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter describes what God said He would do to one nation at one time. It does not issue a command to hate or attack Egypt or any people. The staff of reeds is a charge against Judah's choice of ally, and the lesson for later readers is about where we look for rescue, not about Egyptians. Paul's point in Romans 13:1 that governing authorities hold power under God is a fair companion text, but this chapter is not a template for assessing a modern state's destiny or for reading the news as a code. The 'forty years' is a record of a prophetic figure, not a formula for dating current events. What carries across is the principle: nations that credit themselves with what God gave will be humbled, and believers should not place a weight of trust on a human protector that only God can bear.

debates.question: Was the forty years of Egyptian desolation literally fulfilled?

views.label: A literal, historical period
views.case: Some readers look for a time of devastation after Nebuchadnezzar's campaign, about 568 to 567 BC, and count roughly forty years of reduced Egyptian power until the Persians. They point to the dated, specific nature of the prophecy and to the lists of towns from Migdol to Syene in verse 10.

views.label: A round number for a full generation
views.case: Forty is the Bible's number for a generation and for a complete period of testing or punishment, as in Israel's forty years in the wilderness, Numbers 14:33 to 34. On this view nobody needs a precise tally of empty years. The language is then prophetic description of severe decline, not a census, and Ezekiel's tone matches Jeremiah's gentler 'inhabited as in days of old,' Jeremiah 46:26.

views.label: A pattern that matches Judah's exile
views.case: Egypt's forty years is set against the years of Judah's own judgment and return. Ezekiel 4:6 gives Judah forty days for the iniquity of Judah, each standing for a year, so the number may deliberately place Egypt's discipline alongside Judah's, as one story of God dealing with both.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the point is God's measured judgment and humbling, and that the restoration is real but small. The chapter itself gives the sign of success: Egypt 'will never again exalt itself above the nations,' verse 15.

debates.question: Why does verse 17 give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar for a Tyre that was not fully taken?

views.label: A frank revision of an earlier oracle
views.case: Ezekiel 26 had foretold Tyre's destruction at Nebuchadnezzar's hands, but the long siege did not yield the spoil. Verse 18 openly says the army 'received no wages,' and verse 19 compensates with Egypt. The book shows a prophet adjusting the expected outcome by a later word from the same God.

views.label: The earlier oracle was fulfilled in stages
views.case: Others hold that Tyre did fall in a real sense: Nebuchadnezzar broke its mainland power and forced it to terms, and the wealth had mostly fled by sea. The Egypt oracle then adds a payment for effort, not a correction of Ezekiel 26.

debates.bearing: Either way, God is the paymaster: even a pagan army's labor is, in verse 20, 'done for Me.' Divine promises are never more constrained than human results.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 calls Pharaoh a monster who lies among his rivers. The word for rivers, ye'orim, is the plural of ye'or, a word the Old Testament borrowed from Egyptian for the Nile and its channels, the very river of the boast. The language of the oracle uses Egypt's own vocabulary to take the river out of Pharaoh's hands. The same river word stands behind the Nile's waters turning to blood in Exodus 7, so the plague story is within earshot.

The boast itself is one verb, asah, 'to make' or 'to do', the verb of creation in Genesis 1. 'I made it myself' claims for a king what Scripture reserves for the Creator, which is why the answer in verse 9 and following repeats the boast word for word before it is answered. The Greek Old Testament commonly renders the Hebrew monster, tannin, with drakon, dragon, which prepares the ground for the dragon of Revelation 12:9.

The staff of reeds in verse 6 uses qaneh, a stalk or reed, and the reeds of the Nile are everywhere in Egypt. The picture is that of a walking stick that looks sturdy but splits lengthwise into splinters, wounding the hand that leans on it, as 2 Kings 18:21 says in similar words. A footnote on verse 7 notes that the Hebrew has the clause 'you caused their loins to shake', while the Syriac, Septuagint and Vulgate read 'wrenched,' so the support does not merely give way, it injures the whole back.

The forty years of verses 11 to 13 use the same count that Israel carried in the wilderness, but the restoration of verse 14, which a footnote says could be rendered 'restore the fortunes of Egypt,' uses the idiom of reversing a captivity, language otherwise familiar from promises to Judah.

Finally the horn of verse 21 is qeren, strength or dignity pictured as an animal's horn, and the verb for sprouting is the verb of plants putting forth shoots. A horn that grows like a plant is a mixed image, and the same mixture appears in Psalm 132:17, 'I will make a horn grow for David,' which tells the reader that this promise has the house of David in view. The two verbs of the oracle, the sprouting horn and the opened mouth, are the only gifts it gives to Israel and its prophet, and both are promised for the same day.

typology.type: The monster hooked out of the river, Ezekiel 29:3 to 5
typology.fulfillment: A proud power is caught like a great fish and left on dry ground. The shape appears in the Exodus, where Egypt's king and army are drawn into the sea and drowned, Exodus 15:9 to 10, and in the poetry of Psalm 74:13 to 14 and Isaiah 51:9, where the same God breaks the heads of the dragons. In Christ the pattern becomes cosmic: He shared our flesh and blood so that 'by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,' Hebrews 2:14. The type falls short because Egypt's monster is one nation and a human king, while the final enemy is a spiritual power, the dragon of Revelation 12:9 and 20:2, finally cast down in Revelation 20:10.

typology.type: The staff of reeds that splinters, Ezekiel 29:6 to 7
typology.fulfillment: Egypt as a staff that wounds those who lean on it stands for every human help that cannot bear weight. Isaiah 31:3 says plainly, 'the Egyptians are men, not God.' In Christ the true Staff is found: the Lord who is Shepherd with rod and staff, Psalm 23:4, and the Rock on which a house survives the flood, Matthew 7:24 to 25. Where Egypt hurt Israel's hand, He bears our weight, Hebrews 4:15 to 16. The correspondence is partly by contrast, since it is the failure of the staff that points to the need for the right one.

typology.type: The horn that sprouts for Israel, Ezekiel 29:21
typology.fulfillment: A horn in Scripture is strength, and a horn that sprouts is strength that God brings out of apparent ruin. Hannah's song promised that He 'will exalt the horn of His anointed,' 1 Samuel 2:10, and Psalm 132:17 promised to make a horn grow for David. Zechariah announced the answer: God 'has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69. The escalation is from a hope for national dignity, restored voice and standing, to the personal Saviour born in David's line. The type falls short only in scope: Ezekiel's horn answers the shame of a particular exile, while Christ's answers sin and death.

typology.type: Egypt restored but lowly, Ezekiel 29:13 to 15
typology.fulfillment: A nation judged and then re-gathered as a modest kingdom, with its pride permanently removed, anticipates the fuller promise of Isaiah 19:22 to 25, where Egypt, struck and healed, is called 'My people.' That promise reaches into the New Testament, where Egyptian visitors hear the gospel at Pentecost, Acts 2:10, and where the nations are gathered into the one people of God, Ephesians 2:13 to 19. The correspondence is real, but the type is incomplete, since Ezekiel pictures a limited, earthly rehabilitation while the gospel offers full membership in God's family.

study.christ:
Start with what the chapter does not say. It never names Christ, and the Egyptian setting does not give us license to turn every reed and fish into a code. The links are real but they run along lines the New Testament itself draws.

The first is the horn of verse 21. God promises to make a horn sprout for the house of Israel on the day Egypt's pride is finished. Luke deliberately recalls this when Zechariah praises God for raising up 'a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69. Hannah's song, 1 Samuel 2:10, and Psalm 132:17 had already tied the horn to David's anointed one. When Ezekiel hears that the horn will sprout, he is hearing, in a minor key, the same hope that Mary and Zechariah sing in the opening of the Gospel of Luke. The coming of Jesus is the fulfilment of the thing promised, strength given to a humbled people by God's own hand.

The second is the contrast between the king who says 'I made it myself' and the Son who does only what He sees the Father doing, John 5:19. Pharaoh claims to be the source of the river; Christ, through whom all things were made, John 1:3, receives everything from the Father. Real authority over the waters, shown in His stilling the storm, Mark 4:39, is given and exercised in obedience, not asserted in pride.

The third is the reed. Egypt gave Israel a staff that broke. At Jesus' trial the soldiers put a reed in His hand and struck Him with it, Matthew 27:29 and 27:30, a cruel mockery of kingship, yet the same King bears the weight of a whole world on a wooden cross and does not splinter. He is the help that does not fail those who lean on Him, Hebrews 4:16.

The fourth is the creature dragged out of the water. Hebrews 2:14 says Christ shared flesh and blood so that through death He would destroy the one who holds the power of death. That is the true hooking of the monster, and it was done by a death.

Finally the chapter's last word, a horn and an opened mouth, is a picture of a prophet whose voice is restored among his people. The Word made flesh, John 1:14, is the voice God speaks finally, Hebrews 1:1 to 2. These are not decorations laid over Ezekiel. They are the threads the later writers themselves pull.
study.god:
The chapter pictures a God who owns what nations say they own. Pharaoh claims the river; the oracle answers with a first-person verb and a possessive that belongs to God, 'I am against you and against your rivers,' verse 10. The creator of water and fish is the one who puts hooks in the jaw. The lesson is not that God is jealous of a rival but that He is the only one in the picture who actually made anything.

He is sovereign over empires in a detailed, almost bureaucratic way. Verses 17 to 20 show Him allotting Egypt to Babylon as wages, and notice the sentence 'it was done for Me.' The God who judged Tyre through Nebuchadnezzar does not treat Nebuchadnezzar as a mere tool to be thrown away. He pays him. There is a kind of fairness even in the way God handles an unbelieving army, a justice attentive to what has been spent and owed. This does not make Nebuchadnezzar righteous; it shows that God's accounts include everyone.

He is also a God who judges with a view to knowing. Verses 6, 9, 16 and 21 each end with the recognition formula. Judgment is aimed at teaching, not only at destroying. Even for Egypt there is a day after the forty years, a gathering and a land, even if small. The humbling is permanent, 'never again exalt itself above the nations,' verse 15, but permanence of humility is not the same as permanence of ruin.

He is honest about Israel's own guilt. Verse 16 says that Egypt will serve as a reminder of Israel's iniquity in turning to her. The God of the oracle does not simply stand beside His people against their enemies; He exposes the unfaithfulness of the people who chose a human protector over Him, which is why the same chapter that crushes Egypt also needs a horn for Israel.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to give the credit for every river, harvest and strength to the giver, and to pray as people who know that no ally, however imposing, can carry what God has reserved for Himself. It also invites trust in a God whose word is dated and checkable, since the opening verse gives the precise day it was spoken, a reminder that He acts in actual history.

crossReferences.note: The plague that began the contest with Egypt struck her rivers, canals and reservoirs, the very waters Pharaoh in Ezekiel claims to have made. The Nile is the first place God shows who owns it, and Ezekiel's oracle reopens that argument for a later Pharaoh, so that the old story is heard again.

The Assyrian envoy mocks trust in Egypt as a splintered reed of a staff that pierces the hand that leans on it. Ezekiel borrows the picture almost word for word in verses 6 and 7, but gives it a theological verdict: God Himself says Egypt was never more than a staff of reeds to Israel.

God calls the people who go down to Egypt without asking His advice rebellious children, and says Pharaoh's protection will become their shame. This is the prophetic charge behind Ezekiel 29:16, where Egypt becomes a reminder of Israel's iniquity in turning to her.

The Egyptians are men and not God, their horses flesh and not spirit, and when the LORD stretches out His hand both helper and helped fall together. The line explains why Egypt's wound to Israel and Egypt's own fall happen in the same movement in Ezekiel 29.

The history behind the oracle. Pharaoh's army marched out, the Babylonians briefly withdrew, and Jeremiah said Egypt would go home and the city would burn. It shows the staff of reeds breaking in real time, during the same months of Ezekiel's word.

Jeremiah's oracle against Egypt names Amon of Thebes and those who trust in Pharaoh, delivers them to Nebuchadnezzar, and then adds that Egypt will be inhabited as in days of old. It is a close partner to the restoration of Ezekiel 29:13 to 15, with a softer note.

Earlier Ezekiel had foretold that Nebuchadnezzar would be brought against Tyre. The postscript of Ezekiel 29:17 to 20 returns to that same campaign, so the two passages should be read together as one account of how Tyre's siege led to Egypt's payment.

God promises to make a horn grow for David and prepare a lamp for His anointed. The verb and image match Ezekiel 29:21 and show that the sprouting horn belongs to the line of David, which is how Luke 1:69 reads it.

Zechariah praises God for raising up a horn of salvation in the house of David. This is the New Testament's own answer to the sprouting horn of Ezekiel 29:21, and it moves the promise from national dignity to the Saviour who has now come.

Egypt struck and healed, turning to the LORD and called 'My people.' This sets Ezekiel's lowly, restored Egypt inside a larger hope that reaches beyond rehabilitation to worship and blessing for the nations.

Ezekiel was made mute and told that God would one day open his mouth. The promise in 29:21 that God will open his mouth among the exiles picks up that thread and anticipates 24:27 and 33:22, when his speech is freed at the news of Jerusalem's fall.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story of creation, fall, rescue and renewal keeps returning to Egypt because Egypt is where Israel's story begins as a people and where it learns what God is like. Creation opens with God separating waters and calling things into being, Genesis 1:6 to 10, and the Nile is one of those waters. A king who says he made the river has taken the Creator's place, which is the fall in miniature: the human desire to be the maker rather than the made, Genesis 3:5.

The rescue in Exodus is the great reply. God defeats Pharaoh and brings out a people, 'you will know that I am the LORD,' as the plagues repeatedly put it. Ezekiel 29 is a later episode in the same drama. The same God who struck the Nile now hooks the king of the Nile and leaves him in the desert, and the same people who were rescued from Egypt are found leaning on her again. The reed that splinters is a picture of the fall repeated in every generation: we reach for the help we can see instead of the one who made us.

What the chapter sets up is surprising. After the humbling comes a small restoration, and after the restoration comes a horn. Isaiah 19:22 to 25 stretches that thought to its limit, picturing Egypt, Assyria and Israel as one blessed people. The gospel itself makes room for Egypt, since Egyptians were among those who heard the apostles at Pentecost, Acts 2:10, and the horn promised to Israel is the Saviour of the world, Luke 1:69 and John 3:16.

In the new creation, the rivers are no longer anyone's possession. The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1, and the nations are healed, Revelation 22:2. The Pharaoh who said 'the Nile is mine' is answered by a river that is plainly a gift, and by a city where no one grasps at what was given.

quiz.q: What specific boast provoked judgment against Pharaoh in this chapter?

options.text: He claimed, 'The Nile is mine; I made it myself.'
options.note: Verse 3, repeated in verse 9, gives this exact claim as the provoking sin.

options.text: He refused to send tribute to Babylon.
options.note: Not mentioned as the specific accusation here; the sin named is his boast of self made power over the Nile.

options.text: He built new temples to foreign gods.
options.note: Not described in this text; the accusation concerns his claim over the Nile itself, not temple building.

options.text: He conquered territory that belonged to Israel.
options.note: Not the stated sin; the specific boast condemned is his self sufficient claim over the Nile's origin.

quiz.q: How does the chapter describe Egypt's failure as an ally to Israel?

options.text: As a staff of reeds that splintered and wrenched the backs of those who leaned on it.
options.note: Verses 6 to 7 use exactly this image of a broken, wounding support.

options.text: As a faithful ally who kept every promise of military aid.
options.note: The opposite is described; Egypt is condemned precisely for being an unreliable, harmful support.

options.text: As a nation that never had any relationship with Israel.
options.note: The text assumes a real history of Israel relying on Egypt, which then failed them.

options.text: As a wealthy trading partner with no military role at all.
options.note: The specific image used, a staff people leaned on, points to a military and political support role, not merely trade.

quiz.q: What would happen to Egypt for forty years, according to verses 11 to 13?

options.text: It would be uninhabited and desolate, with its people dispersed among the nations.
options.note: Verses 11 to 12 explicitly describe this forty year desolation and scattering.

options.text: It would enjoy forty years of unprecedented prosperity.
options.note: The opposite is described; the forty years is a period of desolation and scattering, not prosperity.

options.text: It would be ruled directly by Israelite governors.
options.note: Not described in this text; the passage speaks of desolation and later a return of Egypt's own scattered people.

options.text: It would be entirely resettled by Babylonian colonists permanently.
options.note: The text promises the Egyptians themselves would later be gathered back, not permanent replacement by Babylonian settlers.

quiz.q: Why, according to verses 17 to 20, would Nebuchadnezzar be given the land of Egypt?

options.text: As wages for his army's long, costly, and previously uncompensated labor against Tyre.
options.note: Verses 18 to 20 state this directly, tying Egypt's wealth to unpaid Babylonian labor at Tyre.

options.text: As punishment for Nebuchadnezzar's own personal pride.
options.note: The text presents this as a reward, not a punishment, for Nebuchadnezzar.

options.text: Because Egypt had never sinned and this was an unrelated political transaction.
options.note: Egypt's own sin is the subject of the earlier oracle in the same chapter; this is not presented as unrelated to her judgment.

options.text: Because Egypt requested Babylonian protection voluntarily.
options.note: The text frames this as the LORD's sovereign decision to compensate Babylon, not a request initiated by Egypt.

quiz.q: What promise does the chapter give Israel in its closing verse, 21?

options.text: That a horn will sprout for the house of Israel, and Ezekiel's mouth will be opened among them.
options.note: Verse 21 states both of these promises explicitly at the chapter's close.

options.text: That Israel would immediately conquer Egypt themselves.
options.note: No such conquest is promised; the promise concerns a horn of restored strength and Ezekiel's opened mouth.

options.text: That Israel would be permanently exempt from all future judgment.
options.note: Not stated in this verse; the promise is specifically about a horn sprouting and the prophet's mouth being opened.

options.text: That Egypt would become Israel's new capital city.
options.note: Nothing in the text suggests this; the promise concerns Israel's own restored strength, not Egyptian territory becoming Israel's capital.

questions: Pharaoh boasted, 'The Nile is mine; I made it myself,' crediting himself for what only God had given. What resource, ability, or blessing in your life do you quietly credit to yourself rather than to God's provision?
Egypt is pictured as a staff of reeds that splintered and wounded anyone who leaned on it. What have you leaned on for security that, in the end, only let you down or hurt you?

God's justice reached even into the fine details of an international transaction between two pagan empires, paying Babylon with Egypt's wealth. Where do you need to trust that God sees and will settle accounts in situations that feel unfair or unresolved in your own life?

The chapter promises that Egypt would never again be an object of trust for Israel, so they would remember their sin in turning to her. What past mistake or misplaced trust does God want you to remember, not with shame, but as a safeguard against repeating it?

The horn of salvation promised to Israel here finds its fulfillment in Christ, raised up by God's grace rather than human strength. Where in your life right now do you need to remember that your hope rests on God's faithfulness, not on your own or anyone else's self sufficient power?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew tannin, translated 'monster' here, can also mean a large crocodile or serpent, and elsewhere in Scripture describes the primeval chaos creature only God can subdue, Job 41; either sense fits Pharaoh's boastful, godlike self image being exposed as false.

Pathros refers to Upper, or southern, Egypt, considered by ancient Egyptians themselves to be the land of their origin, making the promised return there a deliberate return to Egypt's own ancestral homeland rather than a foreign resettlement.

This verse and the wider oracle in verses 17 to 21 are dated to the twenty seventh year of Ezekiel's exile, making it the latest dated oracle in the entire book, delivered years after the fall of Jerusalem and even after Nebuchadnezzar's long siege of Tyre had concluded.
